warn.text: The Horse family lives in grassy fields and gardens.

attempts.text: The Horse family will need grassy fields and gardens to live.
attempts.reason:
FORMATTING/STRUCTURE (constraint 3): clean pass — exactly one complete declarative sentence, no em dashes, no parentheses, no fragments, and the home is named by family as 'The Horse family'. Read-aloud-safe for a pre-fluent reader; no clause stacking, no hard vocabulary.

VOCABULARY (constraint 2), narrow check: passes. No loss-coded words, no other Wildhaven species named, and 'grassy fields and gardens' is natural-language habitat description rather than a habitat-tag identifier (it does not surface the literal open_grass/cultivated tokens), which is the permitted way to name the habitat at all.

FRAMING (constraint 2), the real failure: the doctrine requires the warning to name the habitat as a present fact — what this family's home *is* — not to project a future deficit. 'will need ... to live' does the latter twice over. 'will need' is future-tense and implicitly counterfactual: it only carries meaning if the player understands the family is about to be without the thing named, so the loss is fully communicated without any banned word ever appearing. That is precisely the implied-loss case a keyword sweep cannot catch. A compliant warn form states the habitat directly, e.g. 'The Horse family lives in grassy fields and gardens.'

TONE (constraint 1), compounding: the trailing 'to live' raises the stakes from habitat to survival. Disclosure copy should tell the player what the home is; 'to live' tells the player what the family will not survive without, which is deterrence pressure and mild emotional leverage rather than a flat factual disclosure. It also sits adjacent to the player's action by construction — the line is triggered by that action, so 'will need ... to live' places the player's choice and the family's need in the same breath without naming either, which is the framing the doctrine forbids.

Not a low score: the sentence is mechanically sound, warm-neutral in register, contains no pleading, no judgment, no urgency markers, and needs only the verb phrase rewritten from a projected need into a present description. Cannot ship as-is.

attempts.text: The Horse family lives in grassy fields and gardens.
attempts.reason:
Passes all three constraint types.

TONE/VOICE: Plain game voice throughout. It is a flat, factual statement of where the family lives, with no pleading, no 'please/poor/sadly/are you sure', no second-person address, no judgment, and no urgency markers (no 'still', 'soon', 'before', 'last'). It reads as disclosure rather than deterrence: it tells the player what this home is without any embedded appeal, and it contains nothing that a later departure or relocation line could refer back to, so it leaves no residue. It also avoids the News Report bulletin register entirely — no headline syntax, no reported-event framing, no colon-and-clause construction.

VOCABULARY/FRAMING: This is textbook warn-line construction under the villager doctrine. It names the habitat ('grassy fields and gardens') and only the habitat; the loss is never named, implied, or gestured at. There is no loss-coded vocabulary ('lose/lost/losing/nowhere/kicked out/vanish/gone/homeless'), and just as importantly no oblique implication of loss — no 'has lived here since', no 'this is the only place', no 'for now', none of the constructions that smuggle in impermanence without a banned word. The player's action is entirely absent from the sentence, so there is no possibility of action and hardship sharing a clause. No other Wildhaven species is named, in noun or adjective form. On the closed-graph rule: the habitat is rendered in natural descriptive English rather than tag identifiers — 'grassy fields' is not the identifier 'open_grass' and 'gardens' is not the identifier 'cultivated' — which is exactly the required technique, since the doctrine demands the habitat be named while the identifiers stay out of player-facing copy.

FORMATTING/STRUCTURE: Exactly one complete sentence, subject–verb–complement, terminal period. No em dashes, no parentheses, no fragments, no semicolons or lists that would break screen-reader cadence. The home is named by family in the required form — 'The Horse family' — and never reduced to 'they' or 'it'. Vocabulary and clause length are well within pre-fluent six-year-old range; 'grassy' and 'gardens' are concrete and picturable, and the coordinated pair 'fields and gardens' is the only structural complexity, which is trivially read-aloud safe.

No issue found that would hold up shipping; the deterministic sweep's clean result is correct here.

attempts.reason:
TONE/VOICE (pass): The line is factual and upbeat, carries no pleading, judgment, urgency, or hedging, and makes no backward reference to the warning — it reads as plain game voice, not bulletin voice.

FORMATTING/STRUCTURE (pass): Exactly one complete sentence, no em dashes, no parentheses, no fragment, and the home is named by family as "The Horse family" rather than "they" or "it." Vocabulary is simple enough for a pre-fluent reader and clean for a screen reader.

VOCABULARY/FRAMING (main deduction): The line correctly frames the family as *finding* a home rather than losing one, and the player's action is entirely absent, so there is no action-adjacent-to-hardship problem and no loss-coded word. Two real weaknesses remain. First, I agree with the deterministic sweep in substance if not in severity: a departure line must carry a destination, and "a new home with wide grasslands and nearby farmland" gives only *attributes* of a destination, never a place the family is going. It describes what the new home is like without ever anchoring where it is, which leaves the destination effectively unnamed — the exact gap the "never leave a family with nowhere named to go" rule exists to close. A destination-bearing construction ("found a new home out past the wide grasslands," "found a new home down where the grasslands meet the fields") would satisfy it with the same word count. Second, "nearby" is unanchored: nearby to what? The most available referent for a player reading this is the player's own plot, which invites a faint causal reading — the family relocated to the edge of the thing the player just did. That is oblique rather than a violation, but it works against the doctrine's insistence that departure copy carry destination and not cause.

On the closed-graph rule I read the line as compliant: "grasslands" and "farmland" are prose paraphrases, not the tag identifiers open_grass or cultivated, and "home" is not the house tag. No other Wildhaven species is named, and "Horse" is the family's own display_name, which the format requires.

Not shippable as-is: fix the missing destination anchor and the dangling "nearby," and this reaches full marks.
